problem: Existing navigation policies are fragmented: static-goal policies are not tested under social constraints, and social navigation methods lack multi-task and cross-platform evaluation. Diffusion-based generative policies (NoMaD, NavDP) have high inference latency, and flow-based FlowNav is static-only and has no coordinate-goal support.
motivation: Real robots need static goal-reaching, exploration and safe traversal of crowds from one policy. Static datasets under-cover the recovery and predictive avoidance behaviours that pedestrian interaction requires. The authors treat static environments as a degenerate case of dynamic ones, so dynamic RL refinement should also help static tasks.
key_idea: Train a rectified-flow (straight-line) generative navigation policy by static imitation learning, then refine it with episode-level GRPO in dynamic crowd simulation, using a new Isaac Sim benchmark with six tasks.
insight: The ablation ladder shows each step adds a gain. Regression to DDPM is a large jump (PointNav SR 53.6 to 77.8), so stochastic multi-modal outputs matter. CFM to RF is a consistent gain (SocialNav SR 60.6 to 62.8, Dyn. Exploration ET 43.8 to 48.0). GRPO post-training helps dynamic tasks most (Dyn. Exploration EA 106.4 to 128.7) and also lifts static PointNav SR from 80.4 to 80.9, supporting the positive-transfer claim, though the static gain is small.
method: Rectified-flow head: learns a constant velocity field u=tau1-tau0 along a linear interpolant between noise and expert trajectories, sampled with K Euler steps (K=6 default), starting from NavDP-pretrained weights.
Multi-candidate critic selection: generates M=16 trajectory candidates and picks the best with a shared critic head.
Stage 1 IL: fine-tunes a 16-layer Transformer decoder (8 RGB history frames + current depth) on 3,000 Gibson trajectories (about 5% of NavDP's data) for 30 epochs.

Stage 2 GRPO: critic-free RL where the M candidates act as the reference group. Uses episode-level Z-score advantages (clipped to [-3,3], gamma 0.99), with updates only at episode boundaries. Trained on SocialNav, Dyn. PointNav and Dyn. Exploration.

Reward design: goal bonus 20, asymmetric progress weight (5 approaching, 2 receding), stuck and timeout penalties, and Hall-proxemics social penalties (0.45 m intimate, 1.2 m comfort). Exploration uses a grid coverage novelty bonus.

Benchmark: Isaac Sim scenes with 20 cluttered training scenes (20k episodes) and 6 structured evaluation scenes (600 episodes). Pedestrians follow a Markov FSM (GoTo/Idle/LookAround) with NavMesh planning and geometric local avoidance. New metrics: S-TL, SC, Coll., MinDist.

setting.backbone: 16-layer Transformer decoder with rectified-flow head + critic head (initialized from NavDP, IL then GRPO fine-tuned)
setting.training_data: Stage 1: 3,000 Gibson trajectories (about 5% of NavDP's ~56k). Stage 2: on-policy RL rollouts in dynamic Isaac Sim scenes (20 ClutterEnv scenes, 20k episodes)
setting.observation: 8-frame RGB history + current depth (RGB-D), goal as point/image/moving agent coordinates
setting.action_space: generated trajectories (waypoint sequences) executed by a low-level controller, robot speed capped at 0.5 m/s
setting.simulator: NVIDIA Isaac Sim (benchmark built on NavDP ClutterEnv and structured scenes); Gibson for IL data
setting.privileged: none stated (real-world uses only a single RGB-D camera)

numbers.extra: Evaluated in the 6 structured Isaac Sim scenes (600 episodes); success radius 1.0 m, 120 s timeout
numbers.evidence: Tab. 1 Performance comparison across six fundamental navigation tasks, PointNav

numbers.extra: Moving-agent goal; pedestrians at 1.1 m/s, robot 0.5 m/s

numbers_note: Benchmark is the authors' own Isaac Sim suite, so splits are labeled 'test' (no official split names). Sensitivity results over M and K are given only as a figure.
results: FLUX beats the strongest baseline NavDP on all six tasks, e.g. PointNav SR 80.9 vs 77.8, SocialNav SR 64.0 vs 59.3 with collisions 16 vs 21, and Dyn. Exploration EA 128.7 vs 93.7. Inference takes 216.5 ms at K=6 vs 305.2 ms for NavDP at K=10. It transfers zero-shot to Go2-W, Go2 and G1 robots.
limitations: No explicit social reasoning (non-verbal intent, etiquette), which limits interpretability.
Evaluation is limited to indoor spaces with simulated scripted pedestrians and a small set of 6 evaluation scenes.
Real-world results are qualitative only, with no quantitative real-robot metrics.
